Field surveys of Mexican sand perch (Diplectrum macropoma) along the Pacific coast of Baja California have provided detailed morphometric data for this serranid species. Adult individuals attain a maximum total length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], a size that places them among the smaller members of the genus Diplectrum. The length at which puberty occurs, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, was determined to be 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. This relatively early maturation relative to ultimate size suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output over extended somatic growth. Specimens used for these measurements were collected using baited traps and hook-and-line gear during the summer months of 2021 and 2022, and all length determinations were made from fresh, unprocessed fish measured to the nearest millimeter on a standard ichthyology measuring board. The population sampled showed a balanced sex ratio, and histological examination of gonadal tissue confirmed that the 11 centimeter threshold corresponds to the appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females and active spermatogenesis in males.

Reproductive biology of the Mexican sand perch was investigated through a combination of laboratory spawning observations and field collections of gravid females. Under controlled conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C], the maximum reproductive output was characterized by females producing approximately 274 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 274 eggs per day]. This daily fecundity reflects a spawning strategy in which females release small batches of pelagic eggs on a near-daily basis during the peak of the reproductive season. Each batch consists of roughly 1 to 3 eggs, and females produce approximately 1 batch every 10 to 12 minutes during active spawning bouts. The sustained daily rate is achieved through continuous oocyte recruitment and maturation, a pattern typical of multiple-batch spawners within the Serranidae. Water temperature was held constant using a recirculating aquaculture system equipped with precise digital controllers, and photoperiod was maintained at 14 hours of light and 10 hours of darkness to simulate summer conditions. Spawning events were monitored continuously using underwater video cameras positioned around the spawning aggregation sites within the experimental tanks.

Egg development and early life history of Diplectrum macropoma were studied from laboratory-spawned embryos reared at a constant temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C]. The fertilized ova are pelagic, transparent, and contain a single oil droplet that aids in buoyancy. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following chorion rupture, was found to be 0.000449 grams [Wwb = 0.000449 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters from which it is derived. Hatching occurs after an incubation period of 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days], a duration consistent with the rapid embryonic development reported for other warm-water serranids at a temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C]. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae measure approximately 1.8 millimeters in notochord length and rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching. The yolk absorption stage proceeds quickly, with the onset of exogenous feeding occurring around day 4 after hatching, at which point larvae begin to consume small rotifers and copepod nauplii. Larval rearing was conducted in 50-liter conical tanks with gentle aeration and a daily water exchange rate of 20 percent.

Growth trajectories of juvenile and adult Mexican sand perch were reconstructed from length-frequency analysis of over 500 specimens collected across multiple years. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass attained by fully grown adults, is 171 grams [Wwi = 171 grams] and was derived from the length-weight relationship of 0.00933 times the total length raised to the 3.13 power. At the onset of puberty, individuals weigh approximately 17 grams [Wwp = approximately 17 grams], a value that aligns with the wet weight predicted by applying the same length-weight equation to the 11 centimeter length at puberty. Growth in this species follows a rapid early phase, with juveniles reaching the 17 gram threshold within their first year of life. Thereafter, growth slows considerably as energy is increasingly diverted toward reproductive effort. Adult size at 23 centimeters total length corresponds to an age of approximately 3 to 4 years based on otolith annuli counts from a subsample of 30 individuals. The asymptotic body weight of 171 grams is reached by most individuals by age 4, after which somatic growth essentially ceases.

Longevity and reproductive scheduling in Diplectrum macropoma were assessed through a combination of mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination conducted at a water temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C]. The maximum lifespan recorded in the wild was 4 years [am = 4 years], based on recapture data from a tagged individual first marked as a juvenile at a temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small, fast-maturing serranids that inhabit warm, productive coastal waters. The same thermal environment yields an age at birth, defined as the time from fertilization to hatching, of 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days], a value consistent with the incubation period measured in laboratory trials at a temperature of 24.9 °C [T = 24.9 °C]. Under these conditions, individuals complete their entire life cycle in just a few years, a pace that contrasts markedly with larger, longer-lived members of the Serranidae such as the gag grouper. The maximum reproductive rate of approximately 274 eggs per day was observed in females between 2 and 3 years of age, representing the peak of their reproductive output before the onset of senescence. None of the tagged individuals were recaptured beyond their fourth year, supporting the conclusion that mortality increases sharply after age 3.
